Tunbridge Wells' population increased by around 300 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population grew very little

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Tunbridge Wells increased by just 0.2%, from around 115,000 in 2011 to around 115,300 in 2021.

The population here increased by a smaller percentage than the overall population of the South East (7.5%), and by a smaller percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Tunbridge Wells was home to around 2.5 people per football pitch-sized piece of land. This area was among the lowest 35% for population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was lower in Tunbridge Wells than across the South East

An older Tunbridge Wells

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Tunbridge Wells increased by three years, from 40 to 43 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than the South East as a whole in 2021 (41 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 50 to 64 years rose by around 2,700 (an increase of 13.0%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 2,800 (10.8% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 50 and 64 years increased by 2.3 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Changing relationships in Tunbridge Wells

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership was greater across the South East (2.9 percentage points) than in Tunbridge Wells (0.8 percentage points).

In Tunbridge Wells, the percentage of adults who had never been married or in a civil partnership increased from 31.3% in 2011 to 32.1% in 2021. During the same period, the regional percentage increased from 31.9% to 34.8%.

The percentage of adults who were married or in a civil partnership in Tunbridge Wells remained at 50.2%, while the percentage of adults who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 9.1% to 9.5%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in Tunbridge Wells increased by 0.8 percentage points

Unpaid care in Tunbridge Wells

In 2021, 4.5% of Tunbridge Wells residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 7.2% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The decrease in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Tunbridge Wells (2.7 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the South East (2.8 percentage points, from 7.3% to 4.5%). Across England, the proportion fell by 2.8 percentage points, from 7.2% to 4.4%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Tunbridge Wells decreased by 2.7 percentage points

Religion in Tunbridge Wells

In 2021, 40.3% of Tunbridge Wells residents reported having "No religion", up from 26.6% in 2011. The rise of 13.7 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Tunbridge Wells. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the South East, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 27.7% to 40.2%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 49.7% of people in Tunbridge Wells described themselves as Christian (down from 62.9%), while 6.3% did not state their religion (down from 8.0% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

Tunbridge Wells residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 97,000 Tunbridge Wells residents said they were born in England. This represented 84.1% of the local population. The figure has decreased from just over 100,700 in 2011, which at the time represented 87.5% of Tunbridge Wells' population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with just over 1,400 Tunbridge Wells residents reporting this country of birth (1.2%). This figure was down from around 1,600 in 2011, which at the time represented 1.4% of the population of Tunbridge Wells.

The number of Tunbridge Wells residents born in countries that joined the EU between April 2001 and March 2011 (other than Poland, Croatia, Lithuania and Romania) rose from just under 700 in 2011 (0.6% of the local population) to around 1,200 in 2021 (1.1%).

In 2021, 84.1% of Tunbridge Wells residents reported their country of birth as England

Health in Tunbridge Wells

In 2021, 52.4% of Tunbridge Wells residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 49.4% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 34.6% to 33.0%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Tunbridge Wells residents describing their health as "very bad" remained 0.8%, while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 3.3% to 2.9%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

In 2021, 0.8% of usual residents said their health was very bad in Tunbridge Wells

National identity in Tunbridge Wells

In 2021, 7.2% of Tunbridge Wells residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 5.6% in 2011.

In 2021, just under 1 in 40 people (2.3%) identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 1.0% in 2011. The percentage of residents in Tunbridge Wells that identified as "British only" increased from 17.0% to 58.3%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK in Tunbridge Wells (1.6 percentage points) was similar to the increase across the South East (1.6 percentage points, from 7.1% to 8.7%). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Tunbridge Wells increased by 1.6 percentage points

Fewer couples without children

Of Tunbridge Wells households, 17.2% included a couple but no children in 2021, down from 19.0% in 2011.

The decrease in the percentage of households including a couple but no children was greater in Tunbridge Wells (1.8 percentage points) than across the South East (1.4 percentage points, from 18.7% to 17.4%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.9 percentage points, from 17.6% to 16.8%.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in Tunbridge Wells decreased by 1.8 percentage points

Fall in employment

Of Tunbridge Wells residents aged 16 years and over, 59.5% said they were employed (excluding full-time students) in 2021, down from 61.1% in 2011.

In 2021, just under 1 in 40 people (2.3%) said they were unemployed, compared with 2.7% in 2011. The percentage of retired Tunbridge Wells residents increased from 20.9% to 22.5%.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed was greater in Tunbridge Wells (1.6 percentage points) than across the South East (1.3 percentage points, from 59.0% to 57.6%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.8 percentage points, from 56.5% to 55.7%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in Tunbridge Wells decreased by 1.6 percentage points

Change in work hours

In 2021, 11.5% of Tunbridge Wells residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week. This figure increased from 10.6% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in seven people (14.5%) said they worked over 49 hours per week, compared with 16.9% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 54.4% to 55.7%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week was greater in Tunbridge Wells (0.9 percentage points) than across the South East (0.5 percentage points, from 10.4% to 11.0%). Across England, the percentage increased by 0.6 percentage points, from 9.7% to 10.3%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in Tunbridge Wells increased by 0.9 percentage points

Change in housing in Tunbridge Wells

Of Tunbridge Wells households, 65.1% owned their home in 2021, down from 65.7% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in five households (19.2%) rented privately, compared with 16.9% in 2011. The percentage of Tunbridge Wells households that lived in a socially rented property decreased from 15.2% to 14.6%.

The decrease in the percentage of households that owned their home was greater across the South East (2.0 percentage points, from 67.6% to 65.7%) than in Tunbridge Wells (0.6 percentage points). Across England, the percentage fell by 2.0 percentage points, from 63.3% to 61.3%.

The rate of home ownership in Tunbridge Wells decreased by 0.6 percentage points

Disability in Tunbridge Wells

In 2021, 5.5% of Tunbridge Wells residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 6.4% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just over 1 in 11 people (9.4%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 8.8% in 2011. The proportion of Tunbridge Wells residents who were not disabled increased from 84.8% to 85.0%.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Tunbridge Wells (0.9 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the South East (1.0 percentage points, from 7.2% to 6.2%). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Tunbridge Wells decreased by 0.9 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Tunbridge Wells

In 2021, 4.0% of Tunbridge Wells residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 2.5% in 2011. The 1.4 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the South East, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 5.2% to 7.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 91.5% of people in Tunbridge Wells identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 94.9% in 2011), while 2.6% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 1.6% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.3% in 2011 to 1.0% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
